extracted.intended_audience: Researchers/authors conducting and reporting in vivo animal experiments (preclinical researchers preparing manuscripts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how to report the design, conduct, analysis and reporting of in vivo animal experiments to maximise transparency, reproducibility, and utility for readers and systematic reviewers. Covers timing, location, rationale, results/statistics, abstract content, background, model choice, objectives, and ethical approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: 9b When and how often
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly report the frequency and timing of experimental procedures and measurements, including the light and dark cycle (e.g. 12L:12D), circadian time cues (e.g. lights on at 08:00), and experimental time sequence (e.g. interval between baseline and comparator measurements or interval between procedures and measurements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that innate circadian rhythms can affect outcomes (behavioural, physiological, immunological). Also report timing and frequency of welfare assessments, taking into consideration normal activity patterns (see item 15 – Animal care and monitoring). If timing varies between animals, provide a supplementary table listing each animal. Examples: (1) vitals and blood samples recorded every 5 minutes at specified timepoints; (2) fasting and clamp schedule with recovery intervals. References provided to illustrate importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 9c Where (including detail of any acclimatisation periods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate where studies were performed (e.g. dedicated laboratory space or animal facility, home cage, open field arena, water maze) and whether periods of physiological or procedural acclimatisation were included in the study protocol, including type and duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: physiological acclimatisation after stressful events (transport) allows stabilisation of physiological responses; procedural acclimatisation before procedures stabilises responses after handling/novel environments. Periods can vary by species and outcome (24 hours to >1 week); standard periods cannot be inferred. If multiple sites were used, state where each experiment and sample analysis was performed. Include accreditation of labs if appropriate (e.g. commercial lab analyses). Examples provided (fish habituation protocol). References support variability and need to report.

rubrics_metrics.name: 9d Why (provide rationale for procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why a particular procedure or technique was chosen, especially when procedures are novel, specific to a laboratory, or constrained by the animal model or equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should give rationale when multiple approaches exist; justify route of administration, model-specific constraints, or methods chosen to avoid bias. Provide examples where route choice (e.g. intraperitoneal vs tail vein injection) was chosen to avoid bias, or why a particular molecular target or method was selected based on prior knowledge. Cite references about routes of administration and other considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 10 Results (report each experiment, including independent replications)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each experiment conducted, including independent replications, report results so readers can evaluate findings and for future meta-analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present results for all experiments, not only representative data. Report the exact number of experimental units per group (see item 2 – Sample size, and item 3 – Inclusion and exclusion criteria). Present data clearly as text, tables, or graphs to enable evaluation or extraction. This header frames the following specific reporting expectations (10a, 10b) and emphasises reporting of all repeats rather than selective presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 10a Summary/descriptive statistics for each experimental group, with a measure of variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Report summary/descriptive statistics for each experimental group, with a measure of variability where applicable (e.g. mean and SD, or median and range).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For continuous data include a measure of central tendency (mean, median) and variability (quartiles, range, SD). Categorical data can be counts, frequencies, proportions. Present data for all experiments and repeats; report exact n per group. Use boxplots (median and IQR) or mean±SD with ranges as appropriate. Examples show standard presentation formats and advise that all collected data are shown where possible to help readers assess precision. References include guidance on displaying data and statistical reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: 10b Effect size with a confidence interval
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicable, report the effect size with a confidence interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that statistical significance (p-values) should not be conflated with biological/clinical importance; effect sizes quantify magnitude and confidence intervals indicate precision. Reporting effect sizes with CIs helps interpret biological relevance, is useful when power is low, and facilitates meta-analysis. Report all analyses performed, including non-significant results. Examples and references illustrate standardisation and presentation of effect estimates with 95% CIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: 11 Abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an accurate summary of the research objectives, animal species, strain and sex, key methods, principal findings, and study conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: a transparent and accurate abstract increases manuscript utility and allows readers to assess reliability; abstracts are used for screening in systematic reviews. Avoid leaving out species, drugs, or other key details. Indicate whether study was hypothesis-testing or hypothesis-generating (see item 13). Include enough detail so readers and systematic reviewers can identify relevant studies. Examples illustrate structured abstract content (background, methods, key results, conclusions). References cite problems with inaccurate/insufficient abstracts and guidance to improve them.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12a Background (sufficient scientific background and rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include sufficient scientific background to understand the rationale and context for the study, and explain the experimental approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate a clear evidence gap and explain why an in vivo approach was warranted. Use systematic reviews where possible to show current evidence and to inform choice of animal model, including benefits and limitations. Describe how the study relates to other research and outline evidence underpinning the hypothesis or objectives. References discuss use of systematic reviews and reporting guidelines to support 3Rs and model selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12b Explain how the animal species and model address the objectives and relevance to human biology
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide enough detail for readers to assess the suitability of the animal model used to address the research question, including rationale for species choice and how outcome measures relate to the condition under study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on stating that a model is commonly used. Explain model validation: how induction of disease is analogous to human condition, response to clinically effective treatments, symptom similarity, and selection of age/sex/health status to represent clinical population. When modelling human disease, indicate appropriateness for specific objectives and validation evidence. Examples include choice of pilocarpine epilepsy model and zebrafish hematopoiesis models. References on model validation and translational reliability are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 13 Objectives (clear research question and hypotheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly describe the research question, research objectives and, where appropriate, specific hypotheses being tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether the study is exploratory or hypothesis-testing; this affects design and analysis (e.g. sample size estimation, predefined primary outcome). Distinguish prespecified hypotheses from those generated after data inspection. Explain primary vs exploratory outcomes. Examples illustrate primary vs secondary objectives and exploratory aims. References on experiment design and distinguishing exploratory/confirmatory research are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: 14 Ethical statement (approval and licences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the name of the ethical review committee or equivalent that has approved the use of animals in this study and any relevant licence or protocol numbers (if applicable). If ethical approval was not sought or granted, provide a justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must state compliance with regulations and guidelines and provide institutional approval details (e.g. IACUC, AWERB) and protocol/project licence numbers. Include any accreditation (AAALAC, GLP) if relevant. If the research is exempt from regulation, explain why and cite international standards complied with. Examples show wording for approvals, permit numbers, and justified exemptions. References discuss implementing reporting guidelines and international welfare standards.
